# Security dilemma and arms races (`security_dilemma_arms_race`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by game_theory, balance_of_power, deterrence
- Core idea: Where no authority stands above states, each must provide for its own safety, and measures taken for defence can change the balance of power. So what one side does to feel safe makes its neighbour less safe; the neighbour answers in kind, and both end poorer and no safer, or at war, although neither wanted it. Thucydides gave the classic case: the growth of Athenian power and the fear this caused in Sparta. The dilemma is sharpest when attack seems to have the advantage over defence and when offensive and defensive preparations look alike. Remedies are transparency, clearly defensive postures (fortresses, not siege trains), agreed limits and reassurance.
- Pitfalls:
  - Not every arms build-up is a misunderstanding; some states do intend conquest, and reassuring them invites attack
  - Arms races do not always end in war; the Anglo-German naval race was effectively decided by 1912
  - Judging the other side by its capabilities while expecting it to judge you by your good intentions
  - Treating it as a modern idea; Thucydides and the Arthashastra both describe it
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Thucydides I.23 on the cause of the Peloponnesian War, and I.90–92 on the dispute over rebuilding Athens' walls; india: c. 1st c. BC – 3rd c. AD – Arthashastra treats every neighbour as a natural enemy whose gain is one's loss; china: 5th–3rd c. BC – Warring States competition in armies, walls and reforms until Qin conquers all; europe: 1898–1912 – Anglo-German naval race; 1950 – John Herz names the 'security dilemma'; 1951 – Herbert Butterfield; 1978 – Robert Jervis on offence and defence
- Read:
  - Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War I.23 and I.88–92
  - John H. Herz, Idealist Internationalism and the Security Dilemma, World Politics 2 (1950)
  - Robert Jervis, Cooperation under the Security Dilemma, World Politics 30 (1978)
